newsitem.title: LIBERIA: West Africans firm on Liberia disarmament deadline.
newsitem.headline: West Africans firm on Liberia disarmament deadline.

text.p: An envoy of West African states trying to end Liberia's seven-year-old civil war says a January 31 disarmament deadline stands and individuals or groups carrying weapons after that date will be forcibly disarmed.

Nigeria's foreign minister, Tom Ikimi, spelt out the tough stand at the end of a visit to Monrovia by a team from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), which expressed disappointment at the pace of disarmament to date.

"After January 31, as stipulated by the peace accord, all warring factions will be deemed dissolved and non-existent and anybody or group of persons carrying weapons do so in their personal capacity and will appropriately face the consequences," he told Reuters late on Saturday.

He said troops of the Nigerian-led ECOWAS peacekeeping force, ECOMOG, had orders to disarm individuals and groups after that date. "This will be done with all the capabilities at its disposal because we are determined to carry on with the next phase which is the electoral process," he added.
The disarmament of the estimated 60,000 fighters under a peace deal agreed in Nigeria's capital Abuja last August is designed to clear the way for elections in May or June.

Earlier, Ikimi told a news conference that Liberia's rival militias were disarming too slowly. "We are concerned at the numerical level of the men disarmed and the quantity and quality of arms collected so far," he said.
U.N. and other monitors say that since the disarmament exercise began on November 22 barely 8,000 fighters have demobilised and about 6,000 weapons have been handed in.
ECOMOG commander General Victor Malu attributed the delay to lack of trust among rival factions but expressed the hope that the disarmament rate would pick up over the next two weeks.
"The fighters are war-weary, the faction leaders can no longer pay them and the package incentives for exchange of arms are attractive, especially for the child soldiers," he said.

West African leaders who brokered the latest deal threatened sanctions against anyone derailing it. A dozen previous deals to end the war, which began in 1989 and has killed well over 150,000 people, collapsed.

The latest deal followed faction fighting in Monrovia in April and May, pitting indigenous ethnic Krahn factions against an alliance incorporating the descendents of the freed American slaves who set up Liberia in 1847 and other indigenous groups.
The descendents of the slaves ruled until a 1980 Krahn coup abruptly ended their stranglehold on power.

Ikimi said Liberia's interim ruling council of state, which on Thursday held its first full session since shooting at the presidential mansion in October, had assured his team "that the meeting signalled a turn for the better".
Faction leaders Charles Taylor and Alhaji Kromah, who have both signalled their intention to run for president, are vice-chairmen on the council.

"We count on the renewed commitment now given to us by the faction leaders that within the next few weeks, we would witness a substantial turn over of weapons and demobilisation of their fighters," Ikimi said.

ECOWAS, he added, would discuss its next moves in Monrovia in the first week of February. Chiefs of staff would assess the disarmament process and nine foreign ministers from a special ECOWAS Liberia committee would discuss election plans.
